title: Intel Interview Experience
author: MAYANK VERMA
body:
Interview Process
Mainly technical and resume-based.
Started with:
Self-introduction
Academic background
Technical interests
My manager went through my resume and asked detailed questions about my projects.
Questions were mainly from:
Computer Organization & Architecture (COA)
Digital Electronics
VLSI fundamentals
Verilog/RTL
Projects mentioned in my resume
Most questions had follow-up questions based on my answers.
Technical Questions / Areas
COA
CPU, ALU, registers, and datapath
Pipelining and hazards
Cache and memory hierarchy
Interrupts and DMA
MMIO vs PMIO
Digital Electronics
Combinational vs sequential logic
MUX, decoder, encoder, adders
Flip-flops and counters
Setup/hold time
Metastability
FSM
Verilog
wire vs reg
Blocking vs non-blocking assignment
Combinational/sequential logic
FSM implementation
Module instantiation
Testbench and debugging
Project-Based Questions
Questions were asked directly from projects listed on my resume.
For each project, be prepared for:
What problem does it solve?
Why did you choose this approach?
Explain the architecture/block diagram.
Explain your individual contribution.
Why did you choose this particular design?
What challenges did you face?
How did you debug/verify it?
What were the results?
What are its limitations?
How can you improve it?
Preparation Strategy
Prepare your resume line-by-line.
Don't mention any technology/project unless you can explain it deeply.
Focus on Digita, CO, Verilo, and your projects.
For every concept, prepare:
What? → Why? → How? → Implementation → Problems → Solutions
Practice explaining projects on a whiteboard, including architecture and RTL.
Focus on understanding concepts rather than memorizing interview questions.

title: Intel Interview Experience
author: MAYANK VERMA
body:
My interview process was primarily technical and resume-driven. The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself and explain my academic background and areas of interest. After that, my manager went through my resume and started asking questions about the projects and technical skills I had mentioned.

The discussion covered Computer Organization and Architecture, Digital Electronics, VLSI fundamentals, Verilog, and project-specific concepts. The interviewer did not just ask direct theoretical questions; many were follow-ups to my answers.

For example, if I mentioned a particular architecture, protocol, Verilog module, or VLSI project, the interviewer would ask why I chose that approach, how it works internally, what happens in corner cases, and how I would implement or debug it.

Therefore, the most important part of my preparation was not memorizing questions but understanding every line of my resume and explaining the concepts behind my projects.

title: Intel Interview Experience
author: RISHIKA YATISHWAR GAUR
body:
How It Started

Intel visited our campus as part of the campus recruitment process for an AI-related role. I was contacted by the HR team at Intel, and my resume was considered for the opportunity.

Round 1 — Resume Shortlisting

The first stage was the resume shortlisting round. My resume was shortlisted based on my academic background, projects, technical skills, and previous work experience relevant to the role.

After the resume was selected, I received a call from the HR team to schedule the interview. The interview was then conducted virtually through a scheduled meeting.

Interview Day Experience

The interview started with a basic self-introduction. The interviewer also wanted to understand my career journey and asked questions such as:

Why did you decide to leave your job and pursue an M.Tech?

Why did you choose this particular branch/specialization?

Tell me about yourself and your previous experience.

After the introduction, the interview moved into technical discussions based on my resume and experience.

1. Resume & Experience-Based Questions

The interviewer went through my resume in detail and asked about the kinds of technical issues I had encountered in my previous work and projects.

I was asked to explain specific problems I had faced, how I approached debugging them, and how I eventually resolved them.

There were also system-design-oriented questions around:

Microservices architecture

System scalability

Latency

Number of requests/hits a system can handle

Overall system architecture

Handling performance-related issues

2. Programming & DSA

The interviewer asked about the programming languages I had worked with and my experience with DSA.

I was asked what I had done in DSA and which concepts I was comfortable with. This was followed by a DSA problem to evaluate my problem-solving approach and coding fundamentals.

3. Project Deep Dive

A significant part of the interview focused on my projects and the technologies I had used.

The interviewer asked questions such as:

What technologies did you use?

Which packages and libraries did you use?

Why did you choose those technologies?

How does the project work internally?

What challenges did you face?

How did you identify and resolve issues?

Which Jira platform/tools did you use for project management?

The discussion was not limited to the high-level architecture. The interviewer also went into implementation and development practices to understand how familiar I was with the technologies mentioned on my resume.

4. MERN & Backend-Related Questions

Since I had mentioned MERN and related technologies, I was asked questions around the development stack and some supporting technologies.

The discussion included:

React Hooks

Lazy loading

Validation schemas

Regex

WebSockets/sockets and their basic working

Apache Kafka and its role in distributed systems

Caching and why it is used

Grafana and its use for monitoring/observability

Backend and microservices architecture

The interviewer also asked how some of these technologies could be used together in a real-world application and how they help with communication, performance, scalability, and monitoring.

5. AI/ML & Technical Skills

Since the role was AI-related, I was also asked questions around Machine Learning and Deep Learning.

The discussion included:

Transformers

LLMs

Tokenization

How transformers work at a high level

Fundamentals of AI/ML systems

The interviewer was interested in understanding both my theoretical knowledge and how well I could explain these concepts practically.

6. Core Computer Science Questions

Towards the end, the interviewer also asked some fundamental Computer Science questions, including:

What is a process?

What is a thread?

Process vs. thread

What is multithreading?

What is multitasking?

How do processes and threads work during concurrent execution?

Overall Experience

Overall, the interview covered a broad range of topics, starting from my career journey and resume, followed by project discussions, DSA, system design, AI/ML, MERN, backend technologies, and core Computer Science fundamentals.

One of my biggest takeaways from the interview was that anything mentioned on your resume can become a discussion point. It is therefore important to understand your projects and technologies beyond just their definitions — including why you used them, how they work internally, the problems they solve, and how they fit into the overall architecture.

Tips

Mention only the technologies and skills you are genuinely confident in, because anything on your resume can become a follow-up question.

Focus on understanding concepts rather than memorising definitions, especially the “why” and “how.”

Prepare thoroughly according to your resume and the job role, and answer questions confidently and clearly.

For SDE/AI/Software roles, have a strong grasp of DSA, especially easy and medium-level problems.

Don’t ignore core CS fundamentals like System Design & Architecture, DBMS, OS, Computer Networks, and OOP.

title: My Intel Interview Experience
author: MUSHFIQUE AZAM
body:
How It Started

I received a call from one of the business units at Intel regarding an opportunity. They first asked whether I was comfortable with C and C++, to which I agreed. Soon after, they scheduled my interview for the following week.

Preparation Strategy

Once the interview was fixed, I reached out to several people working in the semiconductor domain to understand what areas I should focus on. Based on their guidance, I prepared the following topics:

C/C++ fundamentals
OOP concepts
Bit manipulation
Memory management
Operating Systems basics
A quick revision of electronics fundamentals
Interview Day Experience

The interview began with a simple self-introduction.

1. Coding Questions (C/C++)

The interviewer started with hands-on coding questions.

I was asked to demonstrate call by value and call by reference with simple C/C++ code.

Then I got 2 to 3 bit manipulation questions luckily, the same type I had revised earlier.

2. Operating System Concepts

Next came some OS basics:

Concepts around multithreading

I was asked to write a sample multithreading code to show my understanding.

The interviewer seemed satisfied with my explanations and code.

3. Managerial Round Questions

Finally, they asked around 5 to 6 behavioral/managerial questions, such as:

How do you prioritize tasks?

How do you define project deadlines?

How do you handle conflicting priorities?
